WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A distraught, sobbing Afghan Taliban member begged the court for mercy, but got none as an unmoved federal judge here Monday handed down maximum life sentences for convictions on drug trafficking and narco-terrorism charges. A guard watches over a pile of burning drugs in Kabul, Afghanistan, on June 25, 2008. Khan Mohammed, 38, of Nangarhar Province became the first person convicted and sentenced in the United States under a 2006 law that increased the penalty for a defendant found to be involved  with terrorism and distributing illegal drugs. Mohammed, who had been extradited from Afghanistan, was convicted by a jury in May of plotting a rocket attack on U.S. military forces and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. He also was found guilty of distributing between $1 million and $3 million worth of heroin into the United States "to kill Americans as part of a jihad." Mohammed's court-appointed lawyer, conceding that "what he did was wrong," urged U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly to be lenient and sentence his client to only 20 years in prison. Then the full-bearded Mohammed, dressed in an orange jailhouse jumpsuit, addressed the judge. With tears streaming down his face, and choking back his words, he begged for only one or two years. "I have little children and a woman. They depend on me," Mohammed began. "I'm so worried about them." His lengthy emotional appeal went on to include his reason for selling opium. "In my village that's how you have to make a living. There is no house there without opium," he said. Justice Department prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz, however, urged the court to "send a message of deterrence," and warned against "the confluence of drug trafficking and terrorism." "No, he's not the Osama bin Laden of terrorism. No, he's not the Pablo Escobar of the drug world," Stiglitz told the judge. "But this is where the rubber meets the road." Bin Laden is the head of al Qaeda, while Escobar, who died in 1993, was the most powerful of Colombian drug lords. "Afghanistan is ground zero for opium, and an almost limitless source of funds to the Taliban," he argued. Kollar-Kotelly agreed fully with the prosecutors, and strongly admonished the Taliban defendant. "You were convicted 99 percent by your own words," the judge declared, as she recalled how a "courageous" Afghan police chief wore an undercover wire to record Mohammed's plotting. "The fact that no one died is only because you didn't get the missiles you wanted," she said. "In 2006, you celebrated the Americans' use of the opium. It was a jihad. You knew the damage it could cause," the judge continued. "Because of your undiluted hatred for the United States, you might well have launched other attacks had you not been arrested." She added, "Terrorists stand unique among criminals. Deterrence is very important here." Then, concluding dramatically, the judge turned directly to the defendant. "I heard your concerns for your family but no acceptance of responsibility for your action," the judge said. "Defendants often express worry for their families, but if they considered the consequences of their actions beforehand, maybe they would have acted differently."

A security officer stands guard over confiscated narcotics being incinerated in Kabul, Afghanistan, in a June 2008 photo. The defendant, Khan Mohammed, age 38 and hailing from Nangarhar Province, became the inaugural individual both convicted and sentenced within the American justice system under legislation passed in 2006 that toughened penalties for those linked simultaneously to terrorist activity and drug distribution.

Having been sent to the U.S. from Afghanistan, Mohammed faced a jury this past May that found him guilty of orchestrating a missile assault targeting American troops and Afghan citizens at the Jalalabad Airfield. Additionally, jurors determined he had funneled somewhere between one and three million dollars' worth of heroin into America, doing so explicitly "to kill Americans as part of a jihad."

The attorney representing Mohammed, appointed by the court, acknowledged his client's wrongdoing but pressed Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly to show mercy, requesting a comparatively modest 20-year sentence instead.

When given the chance to speak, Mohammed—sporting a thick beard and clad in an orange prison uniform—broke down emotionally before the judge. Tears rolled down his cheeks as he struggled through his words, asking for a sentence of merely one or two years. "I have little children and a woman. They depend on me," he said, expressing deep anxiety over their welfare. His extended, emotional plea also touched on why he had turned to selling opium: "In my village that's how you have to make a living. There is no house there without opium."

Prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz, representing the Justice Department, countered by emphasizing the need to "send a message of deterrence" and cautioning about the dangerous overlap between drug trade and terrorist activity. He clarified, "No, he's not the Osama bin Laden of terrorism. No, he's not the Pablo Escobar of the drug world. But this is where the rubber meets the road"—referencing al Qaeda's leader and the notorious Colombian drug kingpin who died in 1993. Stiglitz further stressed that "Afghanistan is ground zero for opium, and an almost limitless source of funds to the Taliban."

Judge Kollar-Kotelly sided completely with the prosecution's argument, delivering a pointed rebuke to the defendant. "You were convicted 99 percent by your own words," she stated, noting that a "courageous" Afghan police official had secretly recorded Mohammed's scheming while wearing a wire. She observed that casualties were avoided purely by circumstance: "The fact that no one died is only because you didn't get the missiles you wanted." Referencing his past statements, she added, "In 2006, you celebrated the Americans' use of the opium. It was a jihad. You knew the damage it could cause." The judge went further, suggesting that "because of your undiluted hatred for the United States, you might well have launched other attacks had you not been arrested," and emphasized that "terrorists stand unique among criminals. Deterrence is very important here."

In her closing remarks, directed squarely at Mohammed, she noted, "I heard your concerns for your family but no acceptance of responsibility for your action." She continued, observing that defendants frequently voice concern for loved ones after the fact, adding that "if they considered the consequences of their actions beforehand, maybe they would have acted differently."

Khan Mohammed, a 38-year-old member of the Afghan Taliban from Nangarhar Province, has been sentenced to two consecutive life terms after a federal jury convicted him on charges of drug trafficking and narco-terrorism. The sentencing marks a significant milestone in U.S. counter-narcotics and counterterrorism law enforcement efforts, as Mohammed becomes the first individual to be convicted and sentenced under a 2006 statute specifically designed to impose harsher penalties on those who blend terrorism with drug distribution.

The case against Mohammed centered on two interconnected criminal schemes. Prosecutors successfully demonstrated that he had plotted a rocket attack targeting U.S. military forces and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield, an assault that threatened both foreign troops and local noncombatants. In addition to this planned act of violence, the jury found that Mohammed had been instrumental in distributing between $1 million and $3 million worth of heroin destined for the United States. According to evidence presented at trial, Mohammed viewed this drug trafficking operation not merely as a criminal enterprise for profit, but as part of a broader jihad aimed at killing Americans, effectively weaponizing narcotics distribution as a tool of terrorism.

During sentencing proceedings, Mohammed's defense attorney argued for leniency, requesting a 20-year sentence rather than life imprisonment. Mohammed himself made an emotional appeal to the court, tearfully asking for a sentence of just one or two years. He cited the hardships facing his family and explained that his home village's economic survival depended heavily on opium cultivation, suggesting his involvement stemmed from circumstances of poverty and regional dependence on the drug trade rather than pure malicious intent.

However, Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly remained unpersuaded by these pleas for mercy, ultimately imposing the maximum sentence available under the law. In arguing for the harshest possible punishment, prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz emphasized the importance of establishing a strong deterrent against the dangerous convergence of drug trafficking and terrorism. While Stiglitz acknowledged that Mohammed did not carry the same level of infamy or influence as notorious figures like Osama bin Laden or drug kingpin Pablo Escobar, he argued that the case represented a critical opportunity to send a clear message about the severe consequences awaiting those who combine narcotics trafficking with terrorist activities, regardless of their individual stature within these criminal networks.

The verdict and subsequent sentencing underscore the U.S. government's evolving legal strategy in addressing the complex nexus between the global drug trade and international terrorism, setting a precedent for future prosecutions under the narco-terrorism statute.

counterfactuals.output:
**Afghan Taliban Commander Sentenced to Life in Prison on US Narco-Terrorism Charges**

*By CNN Staff*

A senior Taliban-linked drug trafficker was sentenced to life in prison in a Manhattan federal court on Thursday after being convicted of running a massive heroin and opium smuggling operation that prosecutors say funneled millions of dollars to the Taliban to fund attacks against American and coalition forces in Afghanistan.

Noor Mohammad Rahimi, 47, was found guilty in June on multiple counts, including narco-terrorism conspiracy, distribution of heroin intended for importation into the United States, and providing material support to a designated terrorist organization. The sentencing marks one of the most significant narco-terrorism convictions brought by US prosecutors in recent years.

**A Years-Long Investigation**

According to court documents and testimony presented during the six-week trial, Rahimi operated as a key facilitator between opium farmers in Afghanistan's Helmand province and international drug networks, using the proceeds to purchase weapons and pay fighters for the Taliban.

The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), working alongside the FBI and international partners, said the investigation began in 2016 after intercepted communications revealed Rahimi was coordinating shipments of heroin through Pakistan and Iran, ultimately destined for markets in Europe and North America.

"This defendant helped fuel a pipeline of death — not just through the drugs themselves, but through the violence they financed," said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram in a statement following the verdict. "Narco-terrorism is a direct threat to global security, and today's sentencing sends a clear message that we will pursue those who profit from it, no matter where in the world they operate."

**Ties to Taliban Leadership**

Prosecutors alleged that Rahimi held a senior logistical role within the Taliban's shadow government structure, overseeing drug operations in exchange for protection and resources from local commanders. Evidence presented at trial included financial records, intercepted phone calls, and testimony from a cooperating witness who had previously worked within Rahimi's network.

US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Damian Williams, said the case underscored the deep financial ties between narcotics trafficking and terrorism.

"Rahimi didn't just deal drugs — he used the profits to bankroll bombs, bullets, and fighters aimed at American troops and Afghan civilians alike," Williams said in a press conference outside the courthouse. "Today's sentence reflects the gravity of those crimes."

**Defense Argues Case Built on Unreliable Testimony**

Rahimi's defense attorneys had argued during trial that much of the government's case relied on the testimony of a cooperating witness with a history of deception, and that Rahimi was a mid-level trader with no direct command role within the Taliban.

"This is a deeply flawed prosecution," said defense attorney Michael Ference following the sentencing. "We intend to appeal this verdict and continue fighting for Mr. Rahimi."

**Broader Context**

The case is part of a broader US effort to target the financial networks sustaining the Taliban, which has controlled Afghanistan since the withdrawal of US forces in 2021. Afghanistan remains the world's largest producer of illicit opium, though the Taliban has publicly banned poppy cultivation since 2022 — a ban that experts say has been inconsistently enforced and has, in some cases, driven prices higher for existing stockpiles.

Analysts note that narco-terrorism prosecutions like Rahimi's allow US authorities to pursue individuals overseas under extraterritorial jurisdiction, even without a direct US military presence in Afghanistan.

"These cases are incredibly difficult to build, but they remain one of the few tools the US has to hold Taliban-linked figures accountable," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies drug trafficking and insurgent financing. "It's largely symbolic in terms of degrading the Taliban's finances, but symbolically and legally, it matters."

Rahimi was extradited to the United States in 2022 following his arrest in a joint operation conducted with law enforcement in an undisclosed third country. He will serve his sentence at a federal facility, with his legal team confirming plans to file an appeal in the coming weeks.

# Federal Court Sentences Afghan National Under Narco-Terrorism Statute

**NEW YORK** — A federal judge sentenced an Afghan national to 25 years in prison yesterday following his conviction under the 2006 narco-terrorism law, which criminalizes drug trafficking intended to support terrorist organizations or fund acts of terrorism.

The defendant, identified in court documents as a former mid-level opium trader from Helmand Province, was found guilty last spring of conspiring to distribute heroin with the knowledge that proceeds would support an insurgent faction operating in southern Afghanistan.

## The Sentencing Hearing

The federal courthouse was tightly secured for the proceeding, with additional marshals stationed near the gallery. The defendant, dressed in a gray jumpsuit, sat quietly beside his attorney as the judge delivered the sentence.

Addressing the courtroom, U.S. District Judge Miriam Halston did not mince words about the gravity of the offense.

"This is not merely a narcotics case," Judge Halston said. "The evidence presented at trial established, beyond any reasonable doubt, that the defendant knowingly facilitated a pipeline of narcotics proceeds directly into the hands of an organization dedicated to violence against civilians and coalition forces. The law under which this defendant stands convicted exists precisely because the line between drug trafficking and terrorism financing has become dangerously blurred. This court will not treat that blurring lightly."

Assistant U.S. Attorney Daniel Ferris, who led the prosecution, addressed reporters following the hearing.

"This sentence sends an unambiguous message," Ferris said. "Individuals who use the drug trade as a financial engine for terrorism will be pursued, prosecuted, and punished to the fullest extent of American law, regardless of where in the world their conduct originates. The 2006 statute was designed for exactly this kind of case — where narcotics trafficking isn't just a crime against public health, but a direct contribution to organized violence."

During the hearing, Ferris had urged the judge to impose a sentence at the higher end of federal guidelines, arguing that the defendant's role in the network was "instrumental, not incidental."

## Defense Response

Defense attorney Elena Marsh argued for leniency, telling the court that her client had been coerced into participation by local warlords and had no direct ties to attacks on American or allied personnel.

"My client is a farmer's son who became entangled in a system far larger than himself," Marsh said in her closing remarks. "He did not plan attacks. He did not choose targets. He processed and moved a product in a region where refusal often meant death for himself or his family."

Judge Halston acknowledged the defense's mitigation arguments but said they did not outweigh the statute's intent.

"Coercion and circumstance may explain," she said, "but they do not excuse. Congress crafted this law with full awareness that many participants in these networks operate under duress or economic desperation. The statute nonetheless demands accountability, because the harm caused does not diminish based on the trafficker's motive."

## Broader Context

The 2006 narco-terrorism statute, passed in the years following the invasion of Afghanistan, has been used in a limited number of prosecutions, primarily targeting individuals with alleged ties to the Taliban and other insurgent groups reliant on opium revenue.

Legal analysts note that cases under the law remain relatively rare due to the evidentiary challenges of proving a direct link between narcotics proceeds and terrorist financing across international jurisdictions.

The defendant's attorneys indicated plans to appeal the conviction, citing concerns over the extraterritorial application of U.S. law and the reliability of testimony from confidential informants used during trial.

---

*This report is a fictional dramatization created for illustrative purposes. Names, case details, and dialogue are invented and do not depict a real legal proceeding.*

# Federal Court Convicts First Defendant Under Expanded Narco-Terrorism Statute

**CHICAGO** — A federal jury convicted Marco Villanueva-Reyes, 34, on Tuesday of narco-terrorism charges under the amended Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act, marking the first successful prosecution since Congress broadened the statute last year to target cartel-linked fentanyl distribution networks operating within the United States.

Villanueva-Reyes was found guilty on all seven counts, including conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism, distribution of fentanyl resulting in death, and providing material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization—prosecutors successfully linked his distribution network to a Mexican cartel that received the terrorist designation in early 2025.

The case centered on a Chicago-based trafficking operation prosecutors say distributed over 40 kilograms of fentanyl-laced pills across the Midwest, resulting in at least 14 confirmed overdose deaths, including three teenagers from suburban Naperville.

During sentencing, Villanueva-Reyes broke down before U.S. District Judge Patricia Hollenbeck, delivering an emotional statement to the courtroom.

"I never wanted anyone to die. I was trying to survive, trying to send money home to my daughter," he said, his voice cracking as family members wept in the gallery. "I am not a terrorist. I'm not affiliated with anyone's ideology—I was just moving product to feed my family. Please, Your Honor, I'm asking for mercy. My daughter needs her father."

Judge Hollenbeck, who has presided over the federal bench for eleven years, appeared unmoved by the appeal, delivering a pointed rebuke before issuing her sentence.

"The law no longer distinguishes between ideological terrorism and the terrorism of profit when the results are identical: dead children, devastated families, and communities held hostage by poison," Hollenbeck said. "You may not have carried a flag or recited a manifesto, but you were a knowing participant in a supply chain that our government has determined functions as an instrument of terror. Fourteen families will never hear 'I love you' from someone they lost. Your daughter, Mr. Villanueva-Reyes, still has her father. That is a mercy you did not extend to others."

Hollenbeck sentenced Villanueva-Reyes to 45 years in federal prison without possibility of parole, citing sentencing enhancements specific to the narco-terrorism statute.

Legal analysts say the case will likely face appeal on constitutional grounds, with defense attorney Rebecca Sorenson signaling plans to challenge the terrorism designation's application to profit-motivated trafficking rather than ideologically motivated violence.

"This sets a precedent that conflates drug distribution with terrorism in ways that may not survive appellate scrutiny," Sorenson said outside the courthouse. "My client's conduct was criminal, but the terrorism enhancement fundamentally misapplies a statute designed for very different conduct."

The Department of Justice hailed the conviction as a milestone. "This verdict sends an unmistakable message to cartel networks operating on American soil," said U.S. Attorney General's spokesperson David Chen. "Fentanyl trafficking is terrorism, and we will pursue the harshest penalties available under law."

The case is expected to shape prosecutorial strategy nationwide as at least six similar cases currently await trial in federal districts across Texas, Arizona, and Ohio.

**NEW YORK (AP)** — A federal judge sentenced an Afghan national to 25 years in prison Wednesday for conspiring to import heroin into the United States and plotting to attack American forces in Afghanistan with rockets, in a case that prosecutors say highlights the deepening ties between narcotics trafficking networks and Taliban-linked insurgents.

The defendant, identified in court documents as Haji Bagcho Rahimi, 47, was convicted last year following a three-week trial in the Southern District of New York on charges including narco-terrorism, conspiracy to distribute heroin knowing it would be imported into the U.S., and conspiracy to acquire and use anti-aircraft missiles and rocket-propelled grenades against American personnel.

According to trial testimony, Nazari's organization generated an estimated $75 million in illicit proceeds, a portion of which was allegedly diverted to insurgent groups in exchange for protection of drug routes and cultivation areas. Wiretaps, financial records, and testimony from cooperating witnesses formed the backbone of the government's case, painting a picture of an operation that blurred the lines between narcotics trafficking and terrorist financing.

U.S. Attorney Diane Castellano, addressing reporters outside the courthouse, called the sentence a milestone in the fight against narco-terrorism.

"We built this case brick by brick, tracing money through shell companies, hawala networks, and offshore accounts spanning four continents," Torres told the court during sentencing. "The evidence was overwhelming. This was a calculated, profit-driven enterprise that caused immeasurable harm."

Nazari's defense attorney, Elena Marchetti, maintained throughout the trial that her client was a scapegoat within a much larger and more complex regional trafficking system, and that the terrorism-related charges relied on unreliable testimony from witnesses seeking reduced sentences of their own.

"My client has always maintained his limited role in this operation," Marchetti said following the verdict. In her sentencing memorandum, Marchetti urged leniency, arguing that Nazari had no direct role in violent acts and that a life sentence was disproportionate.

"A life sentence effectively erases any hope of redemption," she argued before the court. "My client is a product of a broken system, not the architect of terrorism. We respectfully ask this court to consider a sentence that reflects proportionality and the possibility of rehabilitation."
